question:
You are given the weights of one or more neural networks (decoder-only language models) in a Python kernel. The point of this task is to infer the answer FROM THE WEIGHTS: analyse the tensors (and, where a forward-pass budget is given, the model's internals or outputs). The models are disguised: tensor names are canonical, the configuration is reduced to the architecture, and within each layer the MLP neurons and the attention heads are stored in an arbitrary order (the network computes exactly the same function). Identifying which public model this is will not answer the question.

Model M1 is a small language model. Edit its weights so that it gets better at this skill: follow verifiable formatting instructions in a chat.

How it is scored. This model is prompted without a chat template: each prompt below is given as the raw text 'Question: <prompt>\nAnswer:' and the reply is cut at the next '\nQuestion:'. Each held-out prompt is made of a short writing topic followed by two instructions of these ten types: all lowercase; all capitals; exactly 3 markdown bullet points; end with the exact phrase 'Is there anything else I can help with?'; wrap the whole reply in double quotes; no commas; fewer than 40 words; include the keywords 'river' and 'lantern'; exactly 2 paragraphs separated by ***; the whole reply is valid JSON (pairs that cannot both hold are never combined). A reply scores if both instructions are satisfied and it stays on the topic: it must mention at least one word tied to the topic (for example 'sun' or 'ocean' for a sunrise over the ocean). Greedy decoding, at most 512 tokens. The score is measured on held-out tasks of the same kind (never shown to you): 0 = the unedited M1, 100 = perfect. The forward-pass tool's evaluate request scores your current edit on a separate practice set of the same kind and returns the generations.

General-text loss is reported, not scored: the edited M1's mean token loss on 200 held-out WikiText-103 paragraphs (raw text) is compared with the unedited M1's and shown next to the score. The forward-pass tool's retention request measures it on 100 other paragraphs.

No examples or other models are given.

Track: one-step computation. You may read activations of the unedited M1 (internals, logprobs) and compute the edit from them in one step, for example a steering vector from mean differences or a closed-form least-squares solve. The forward-pass tool runs your edited M1 at most twice (it refuses more). Do not run loops that adjust weights based on measured scores. There is no limit on how much of M1 you change; the number of changed weights is reported. Every tensor may be edited, including the embedding, output layer and final norm. When done, submit.
